cards.title: Zig v0.17.0

depth.text: Zig's latest release **reworks its build system** and **changes how several language features behave**

The release includes five months of work from **206 contributors** across **925 commits**. It introduces the Build Server Protocol, and the ELF linker was improved so **incremental compilation** is expected to work for everyone on x86_64-linux. The new @bitCast definition may break existing array or vector casts without a compile error, so the notes suggest auditing them when upgrading.

cards.camps: Two camps: some welcome using LLMs to find bugs as a pragmatic tool; others say Zig's community has treated people poorly over LLM use.

comments.text: Would recommend checking out the Zig state of the (tagged) union as well. https://youtu.be/zwi5b5xSsKA?is=PTjJJjSnVMdRuZag It may surprise some people here to see that Andrew is warming up to using LLMs to discover bugs (inspired by results from SQLlite) and considers it a tool on the path to getting to bug free software.

I’ve written software for a living in JS, C, Pascal, and Go, and I’ve tried many, many more languages. After working on a project in Zig for a year, I’m convinced that Zig is the best-designed language I’ve tried so far. Haskell comes close. At least, it’s the best-designed language for humans. It’s not for everyone yet. It’s still unstable, and its ecosystem is small. However, both are improving.

I'm always impressed by Zig's targets support. I'm starting to think that it might be the only language that competes with C on this regard. I'm looking forward to see what the new build integration can unlock on the tooling side. What I'm looking for the most for the next release(s): - New stackless coroutine IO implementation - First class fuzzer tooling

I left the zig eco-system due to zig core members hostile behaviour toward humans not just LLM, so good to see the change they are becoming pragmatic. depth.text: someone got **Linux running** on an M4 Mac with **all CPU cores** by replacing broken sleep instructions

The M4’s **WFI behavior** could make cores **lose CPU state**; replacing WFI and WFIT with NOPs let Linux boot with all cores enabled. That workaround has since been **merged into mainline Linux and m1n1**, so their latest releases can boot natively with secondary cores on M4 Macs.

glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.HTML4: An older set of rules for making webpages.
glossary.CSS: Cascading Style Sheets: rules that control how a web page looks.
glossary.marquee-scroll: A CSS effect that makes text scroll across a webpage.
glossary.domain squatting: Registering a web address mainly to profit from someone else’s interest in it.
glossary.Flash: A technology used to make games and animations that played in web browsers.
glossary.Ruffle: A tool that lets old Flash games run without Flash.
glossary.BBS: Bulletin Board System: an online place people used to post messages and share files.
glossary.tokens: Small pieces of text an AI counts as it reads or writes; they can affect how much a request costs.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.vibe coding: Making software by telling an AI what you want and letting it write the code, often without closely checking how it works.
glossary.agentic patterns: Ways of setting AI helpers to carry out work, sometimes by giving them separate jobs like planning, building, and reviewing.
glossary.inference provider: A service that runs an AI model and sends its replies to an app.
glossary.open-weight model: A model whose trained settings are shared so other people can use them.
glossary.context window: The amount of text and information an AI can take into account at one time.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.brutalism: A style of architecture known for stark, concrete buildings.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.FBX: A file type used to move 3D models between programs.
glossary.OBJ: A file type for saving and moving 3D models.
glossary.WFC: Wave Function Collapse: a way for a computer to build patterns by choosing pieces that fit together.
glossary.Unity: A program people use to make games.
glossary.creative mode: A Minecraft setting where you can build freely without the usual resource-gathering and survival limits.
glossary.sensitivity settings: Controls for how quickly your view turns when you move the controller.
glossary.block granularity: Building in block-sized pieces, which can limit how much detail you can show.
glossary.Java mod: A player-made change to Minecraft that can add things or change how the game works.
glossary.UBI: Universal Basic Income: money regularly given to people without requiring them to work for it.
glossary.Bedrock Edition: A different version of Minecraft, which a commenter asks why Tomlin is using.
glossary.interpolated frames: Extra in-between images made to make separate observations look like smoother motion.
glossary.coronagraph: A device that blocks a star’s bright light so nearby planets can be seen.
glossary.exoplanet: A planet that orbits a star outside our solar system.
glossary.Build Server Protocol: A shared set of rules that lets build systems communicate with other programs.
glossary.ELF linker: A tool that joins compiled pieces of code into a program, using a format common on Linux.
glossary.incremental compilation: Rebuilding only the parts of a program affected by changes, rather than starting over.
glossary.@bitCast: A Zig operation that reads the same bits as a different type.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.kernel: A small program that carries out a calculation on a computer's graphics chip or processor.
glossary.pattern matching: Spotting familiar shapes or arrangements and using them to guess what fits.
glossary.cell identity: The traits that make a cell one kind of cell rather than another.
glossary.methylation: A chemical tag on DNA that can affect whether a gene is active.
glossary.de methylation: Removing chemical tags from DNA, which can affect whether a gene is active.
glossary.Hayflick Limit: The limit on how many times a cell can divide before it stops dividing.
glossary.epigenetic aging: Aging linked to changes in which genes are active, rather than changes to the genes themselves.
glossary.circadian rhythms: Your body's repeating daily timing for things like sleep and waking.
glossary.reinforcement learning: A way to train an AI by rewarding choices that work and discouraging choices that do not.
glossary.imperfect information game: A game where players must make choices without seeing all the information that could affect the outcome.
glossary.silent defense: A Stratego version where the defender keeps a piece's number hidden after an attack.
glossary.inference engine: Software that runs a trained AI model on input so it can produce a result.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.mixture-of-experts (MoE): Mixture of Experts: an AI design that sends each request to only some of a model’s specialized parts.
glossary.asymmetric quantization: A way to shrink a model by storing selected parts with less precise numbers while keeping other parts more precise.
glossary.KV cache: A store of earlier model calculations that it can reuse instead of doing them again.
glossary.SSD: Solid-state drive: storage that keeps files even when the machine is turned off.
glossary.CLI: Command-Line Interface: a way to control a computer by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
glossary.GGUF: GPT-Generated Unified Format: a file type for saving an AI model so compatible programs can use it.
glossary.FFI: Foreign Function Interface: a way for code in one language to call code written in another.
glossary.prefill: The part of an AI request where it reads the prompt and earlier conversation before writing its answer.
glossary.generation: The part where a model writes its reply.
glossary.face: A person's public respect and standing in a group, which can be damaged by embarrassment.
glossary.Dark World frame: A way of seeing people as mostly self-interested and likely to harm you, so strength seems safer than kindness.
glossary.bullet comments: Viewer comments shown over a video as it plays, so you read them while watching.
glossary.AGI: Artificial General Intelligence: a hypothetical AI that could handle many kinds of tasks, not just one narrow job.
glossary.SDK: Software Development Kit: tools a company provides so people can make apps for its device.
glossary.ESP32: A small computer board that can connect to Wi-Fi and control electronics.
glossary.firmware: The built-in software that tells a device's hardware how to work.
glossary.actuator: A part that turns a command into movement, such as steering or braking.
glossary.IoT: Internet of Things: everyday devices connected to the internet so they can share information or be controlled remotely.
glossary.local HTTP API: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Application Programming Interface: a way for software on your home network to ask a device to do something.
glossary.WFI: Wait For Interrupt: an instruction that lets a processor pause until it has something to handle.
glossary.WFIT: Wait For Interrupt with Timeout: a pause instruction that also sets a time limit for waiting.
glossary.NOP: No operation: an instruction that tells the processor to do nothing.
glossary.MMIO: Memory-mapped input/output: a way for software to talk to hardware by reading and writing certain memory addresses.
glossary.MMU: Memory Management Unit: hardware that helps an operating system manage memory and keep programs separate.
glossary.device tree: A file that describes a device’s hardware so Linux knows how to work with it.
glossary.m1n1: A tool used here to start Linux and help inspect Apple hardware.
glossary.SPTM: Secure Page Table Monitor: a security feature that helps protect the macOS kernel from vulnerabilities.
glossary.RVBAR: Reset Vector Base Address Register: a memory location that tells a CPU core where to start running after it powers on.
glossary.hypervisor: Software that lets one computer run another operating system in a controlled environment.
glossary.SoC: System on a Chip: a computer’s main processing parts built together on one chip.
glossary.Full Disk Access: A Mac permission that lets an app reach files it would otherwise be blocked from opening.
glossary.AI agent: An autonomous computer program that can carry out tasks.
glossary.ecological study: A study that looks for patterns across groups or places, instead of following each person.
glossary.covariate: A factor researchers account for while looking at another pattern.
glossary.proximity score: A number based on how close a place is to a site, with nearer places counting more.
glossary.relative risk: How likely an outcome is in one group compared with another.
glossary.Attributable Fraction: A study’s estimate of what share of an outcome can be assigned to a particular factor.
glossary.association: A pattern where two things show up together, which alone doesn’t show that one caused the other.
glossary.causality: The idea that one thing actually makes another thing happen.
glossary.overfit model: A method that fits the examples it was built from too closely, so it can give misleading answers elsewhere.
